```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
library(mortensor)
```

## Data

### How do I bring my own data in?

`mt_data()` takes long data frames, one row per cell, with a column for
deaths, exposures or population and columns for age, period and strata.
Ages can be single years, labels such as `"<1"`, `"01-04"`, `"85-89"`,
`"90+"`, `"85 and over"`, or two columns with lower and upper bounds:

```{r}
parse_age_labels(c("<1", "01-04", "85-89", "90+", "85 and over"))
d <- data.frame(region = "A", year = 2019, age = c("85-89", "90+"), deaths = c(120, 210),
                exposure = c(2500, 1400))
mt_data(deaths = d, exposure = d, by = "region")
```

Deaths and exposures may come at different resolutions (for example deaths
in 5-year groups, exposures by single year of age). Tables in wide format,
with one value column per sex or cause, are read by listing the columns
(`value = list(deaths = c(female = "Female", male = "Male"))`). Values
given as text with symbols for suppressed or missing cells (`"."`, `"x"`,
`"-"`) are recognised; other symbols are declared with `missing` and
`zero`. Readers exist for Human Mortality Database tables (`mt_from_hmd()`,
`mt_read_hmd()`), GENESIS and GBE-Bund exports from Destatis
(`mt_read_genesis()`, `mt_read_gbe()`), `StMoMoData` and `demogdata`
objects (`as_mt_data()`).

### I have populations on 31 December, not exposures. What now?

Read them as `population` and convert them with `mt_as_exposure()`, whose
`type` says what the counts are: `"dec31"` for populations on 31 December
(the exposure of year t is the mean of the populations on 31 December of
t - 1 and t), `"jan1"` for populations on 1 January, `"midyear"` for
mid-year estimates. Exposures are the denominator of the rates, so this
choice matters for the level of every forecast.

### What does `mt_validate()` check?

Cells with zero exposure, deaths without exposure, death rates above one
below age 100, missing values, strata without deaths or exposures, levels
that look like totals of other levels (for example `"Insgesamt"` among the
regions), grid cells without observations, and, with a hierarchy, whether
totals equal the sums of their parts (deaths and exposures add up over
regions or sexes; rates add up over causes,
`mt_hierarchy(cause = list(total = "all", additive = "rates"))`).

## Granularity and ungrouping

### Should I model single years of age or the age groups of my data?

Model at the resolution the question needs. Life expectancy, probabilities
of dying and age-standardised rates can be computed from 5-year groups (the
life table uses the interval widths). Single years are needed when results
are reported by single year, when a model needs them (cohort models such as
APC need equal age and period steps), or when data at different
resolutions are combined. Backtests always score against the deaths at
their observed resolution, so ungrouping errors count against the model,
and `mt_backtest()` with and without `step_ungroup()` answers the question
for your data.

### Which ungrouping method should I use?

The penalized composite link model (`mt_ungroup()`, default) ungroups
deaths as rates with the exposures as offset. Its estimates are the
fitted values of the model: they reproduce the total over all age groups
of a fit, and the diagnostics report the largest gap to a single group
total (`max_rel_diff`). `preserve_totals = TRUE` rescales the estimates
to every group total, a post-hoc rescaling of this package that creates
jumps at the group boundaries. `method = "monotone"` interpolates the
cumulative counts and reproduces every group total, without using the
exposures.
The spline methods `"hyman_kannisto"`, `"natural_gompertz"` and `"gam"`
are deprecated: they have no published source. Check your own result
with `mt_plot_ungroup()` and `mt_ungroup_check()`; see "Ungrouping age
groups: methods and diagnostics".

### Can I split the open interval 90+ into single years?

Only from assumptions: the data say nothing about the age pattern inside
the interval. `mt_ungroup()` warns when it extrapolates. Prefer a grid
whose open interval starts where the data's does, or data with a higher
open age (for example exposures to 100+ with deaths to 90+, where the
exposures carry the age pattern).

## Models and uncertainty

### Which model should I use?

There is no single best model; a rolling-origin backtest on your own data
(`mt_backtest()`, horizons like the ones you will report) decides. As a
starting point:

| Situation | Try first | Why |
|---|---|---|
| One population, many deaths per cell, single years or 5-year groups | `lee_carter()`, `rwd()` and `ensemble(lc = lee_carter(), rw = rwd())` | Lee-Carter is the standard; single models give too narrow intervals on real data, the ensemble is better calibrated |
| Several strata that should not diverge (sexes, regions, deprivation groups) | `li_lee(common_by = ...)` | a common trend with bounded deviations; pools information across strata |
| Small populations, many cells with few deaths | `li_lee(common_by = ...)`, wider age groups (`mt_regroup()`), `step_smooth()`; `arima_series(order = c(0, 1, 1), drift = TRUE)` in ensembles | pooling and smoothing reduce noise; the plain random walk accumulates it, the random walk observed with noise separates it from the trend |
| Totals and parts must add up | `reconciled(model, hierarchy)` | bottom-up for joint models, WLS for separate models |
| Causes of death | separate or Li-Lee models per cause, `reconciled(..., method = "bottom_up")` with `cause = list(total = "all", additive = "rates")`; `coda_causes()` (experimental) | cause rates add up to the all-cause rate |
| Cohort effects (for example generations born around 1925-1945) | `apc_bayes()`, `stmomo("apc")` | age-period models attribute cohort patterns to period trends |
| Trend change in the recent past | `step_window(years)` with a backtest of several windows | a shorter fitting period follows the recent trend |
| Long horizons, as mortality falls most at ever older ages | `lee_carter(rotate = TRUE)`, `coda()` | the rotation moves the age pattern of decline to older ages as life expectancy rises (Li, Lee and Gerland 2013); CoDa forecasts the distribution of deaths by age (Oeppen 2008) |

Check every fit with `summary(fit)`, `mt_parameters(fit)` and
`mt_plot_residuals(fit)`, and every forecast for warnings about
implausible rates.

### Why are my 95% intervals too narrow (or too wide)?

Intervals of most models describe the uncertainty of their own
assumptions, for example a constant drift, and their predictive draws add
the Poisson variation of the deaths only. On real data, changes of trend
and year effects add uncertainty that these assumptions leave out, so
intervals tend to be too narrow over 5 to 10 years: in the backtests of
the vignettes the 95% coverage of Lee-Carter was 0.79 on the ONS
quintiles (horizons 1 to 5, "Getting started with mortensor") and 0.63 on
England & Wales men (horizons 1 to 10, "Tuning and recalibration"). The
plain random walk is wider, because year-to-year changes of observed
rates contain observation noise twice; the local level model with drift,
`arima_series(order = c(0, 1, 1), drift = TRUE)`, separates the noise
from the trend (Harvey 1989). Mixtures of models (`ensemble()`) widen the
intervals where the models disagree, and the negative binomial family of
`stanmomo()` allows for overdispersion. `recalibrated()` rescales the
spread of any model's draws to its forecast errors in the last years of
the training data (by default ten); on England & Wales men it raised the
95% coverage of Lee-Carter from 0.63 to 0.85. Check calibration with
`mt_backtest()` and `mt_plot_coverage()`.

### Is one model really more accurate than another?

A backtest gives mean scores from a few origins, and two models often
differ by less than these scores vary between origins. `mt_dm_test()`
tests whether the difference is larger than chance, horizon by horizon,
with the Diebold-Mariano test (Diebold and Mariano 1995). By default the
long-run variance of the loss differences is the equal-weighted cosine
estimate with fixed-smoothing critical values (Lazarus et al. 2018;
Coroneo and Iacone 2020), which allows for the overlap of forecasts from
neighbouring origins and keeps the size of the test nearly correct with
few origins:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bt <- mt_compare(list(lc = lee_carter(), rw = rwd()), data, origins = 1995:2009, h = 5)
mt_dm_test(bt, ref = "lc")
```

With few origins the test has few degrees of freedom and finds only large
and consistent differences. More origins, or origins spaced `h` years
apart, whose forecasts do not overlap, give more informative tests.
`varestimator = "acf"` gives the test of `forecast::dm.test()` with the
small-sample correction of Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold (1997); with 7
overlapping origins it rejected a true null hypothesis in 10% to 19% of
simulated samples at the nominal 5% level (see `?mt_dm_test`). A
non-significant difference means that the backtest cannot tell the models
apart; they may still differ.

### How do I choose smoothing and model parameters by forecast accuracy?

This is tuning: fit each candidate setting to the years up to `T - h`,
forecast the last `h` years, and keep the setting that forecast them best,
then refit it to all years. `mt_tune()` does this for any grid of
settings, including preprocessing, and `tuned()` makes it part of a model,
so that an outer backtest repeats the choice at each origin without seeing
the test years:

```r
grid <- expand.grid(k = c(10, 30), order = 1:6)
spec <- tuned(function(order, k) hyndman_ullah(order = order, smooth_args = list(k = k)), grid,
              inner_origins = 1, inner_h = 10, metric = "rmse")
```

`inner_origins = 1` is a single hold-out of the last ten years; several
origins (`inner_origins = 3, inner_h = 5`) average over more periods.
`metric = "rmse"` chooses by point accuracy, `"crps"` by the whole
forecast distribution, and `target = "life_expectancy"` by the quantity of
interest. `recalibrated()` answers a different question: it keeps the model
and rescales the width of its intervals to the recent forecast errors. The
two combine as `recalibrated(tuned(...))`.

### Should I smooth the data before forecasting?

Smoothing over age can help where cells hold few deaths (rare causes,
small regions); check it in a backtest, as the applied vignettes do.
Smoothing over time removes the year-to-year noise from the fitted trends
and from the start of the forecast, but also the variation from which
models such as Lee-Carter estimate the uncertainty of their period index:
on the ONS quintiles, Whittaker smoothing over time lowered the 95%
coverage of Lee-Carter from 0.80 to 0.63 and raised its CRPS from 0.067 to
0.072 ("Smoothing death rates"). `recalibrated()` re-estimates the spread
of a smoothed model against the raw observations. Treat smoothing as
optional and check it in a backtest. Use it as a preprocessing step
(`mt_prep(step_smooth(...))`), never on the data before fitting
(`mt_backtest()` stops, `mt_fit()` warns), so that backtests refit it on
each training window and residuals and scores refer to the raw rates.
`mt_smooth_check()` and `mt_plot_smooth()` show what the smoothing
removed.

### Why does the forecast start with a step?

Most models start from their fitted rates of the last observed year. When
the fit misses the level of the last years, the first forecast year jumps
away from the observations; `mt_jump_off()` reports the step, and the
forecast plots show it as a gap between the solid (fitted) and the dashed
(forecast) line. `anchored(model)` starts any model from the observed
rates of the last training year and keeps this offset in every forecast
year, the jump-off adjustment of Lee and Miller (2001);
`lee_carter(jump_off = "observed")` and `li_lee(jump_off = "observed")`
do the same within the model. The observed rates of one year carry their
random variation into every forecast year, which matters where deaths are
few. The other settings of `anchored()` are package-specific: the offset
of the last `years` years, shrunk where deaths are few (`shrink = TRUE`)
and fading out over `decay` years. "Where a forecast starts: the
jump-off" compares the starting points in a backtest. Decompositions of a
change from an observed to a forecast year include the step;
`mt_decompose()` reports it (`jump_off`) and can start from the fitted
rates (`observed = "fitted"`).

### What is the difference between predictive draws and forecast rates?

For models of expected rates (Lee-Carter, Li-Lee, CoDa, Tucker3, FDM,
StMoMo, StanMoMo, Bayesian APC), `mt_forecast()` returns draws of the
expected death rates by default, and `predictive = TRUE` draws the deaths
given these rates and the exposures, which is what an observed future
rate will show. The deaths are Poisson, the observation model of the
Poisson Lee-Carter model (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002), or negative
binomial for `stanmomo(family = "nb")`; no other observation noise is
added. Models of observed rates (`rwd()`, `arima_series()`,
`ets_series()`) forecast observed rates directly, and `predictive` adds
nothing unless they were fitted to smoothed rates. Backtests use
predictive draws because they are compared with observed rates. For life
expectancy and other summaries of the underlying mortality, use the
default draws.

### How do I handle small populations and zero deaths?

Models that take logs of observed rates (the random walk, the SVD
version of Lee-Carter, Li-Lee) replace zero deaths by 0.5, which is
harmless for a few cells and distorting for many. The Poisson Lee-Carter
gives age groups without any death a constant rate and shrinks the age
pattern of change where the counts are too sparse, with a warning (both
are safeguards of this package). With many small cells:

* model at a coarser resolution (age groups instead of single years, or
  wider groups at young ages, `mt_regroup()`);
* pool information across strata, for example `li_lee(common_by = "sex")`
  for regions or deprivation groups, or borrow strength across ages and
  years within a stratum with the smoothing priors of `apc_bayes()`;
* smooth before fitting with `step_smooth()` (age 0 is left out by
  default);
* use the local level model with drift, a random walk observed with
  noise (`arima_series(order = c(0, 1, 1), drift = TRUE)`; Harvey 1989),
  instead of `rwd()`, alone or in an ensemble: the plain random walk
  treats the Poisson noise of observed rates as real change, and its paths
  over 10 or more years can reach impossible rates;
* combine rare causes of death into larger groups (see `ons_cause_groups`
  and `mt_group_levels()`).

`mt_forecast()` warns when forecast death rates exceed 1, the clearest sign
that a model is unstable for the data.

### Which function aggregates what?

| Function | Combines | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `mt_regroup()` | ages or periods | single years to 5-year groups, or to the groups of another table |
| `mt_group_levels()` | levels of one stratum variable, replacing them | deciles to quintiles, causes to cause groups |
| `mt_aggregate_strata()` | strata along a hierarchy, adding totals and groups as new strata | regions to East, West and Germany, sexes to both sexes |
| `mt_aggregate_draws()` | forecast draws along a hierarchy or to wider age groups | forecasts for Germany from forecasts by Land |

### How should I treat the COVID-19 years?

Either end the training data in 2019 (as in the ONS vignettes), or mark the
years as shocks so that the trend is estimated without them:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
prep <- mt_prep(step_shocks(2020:2022, action = "interpolate"))
fit <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), data, prep = prep)
```

Whether mortality returns to the pre-pandemic trend is an assumption the
model does not test.

## Coherence

### How do I get forecasts that add up over regions, sexes or causes?

Describe the structure with `mt_hierarchy()` and either model the bottom
strata and sum them (`reconciled(..., method = "bottom_up")`), or model
every node and reconcile the draws (`method = "wls"`, `"mint"`, ...).
Totals that are not in the data are added by `mt_aggregate_strata()`.
To keep a trusted total, such as an all-cause forecast that the causes
must add up to, give it as `fixed` and use `method = "proportional"`
(its parts are scaled in proportion to their forecasts) or `"wls"` (the
most uncertain parts absorb the difference). `method = "energy_score"`
learns the reconciliation from the base model's past forecasts
(Panagiotelis et al. 2023); in the package's backtests it was less
accurate than `"wls"`, so compare it in a backtest before using it. Over long horizons, sums of
cause forecasts tend to be more pessimistic than forecasts of all causes
(Wilmoth 1995), so compare the two before choosing. Reconciliation of
deaths uses exposures of the forecast years; supply
population projections as `exposure` when they are available. See
"Coherent forecasts: totals and their parts" and the applied vignettes
"Inequality in England" and "Differences between the German Laender".

### Will the gap between regions or deprivation groups keep growing?

That depends on the model, not only on the data. Separate models per
stratum extrapolate each stratum's trend, so gaps can widen without bound.
`li_lee()` and `coherent_fdm()` let strata deviate from a common trend
only through stationary processes, so gaps return towards their past
level; so does `coda(coherent = TRUE)` for the distribution of deaths by
age. Backtests over a few years rarely separate the two; the choice
is an assumption to state.

### Which ages and causes explain a gap, and how much is composition?

`mt_decompose()` splits a difference in life expectancy (or in the
probability of dying, an age-standardised or crude rate, or any function
of the rates) into contributions of ages and causes: between strata in one
year (`var`, `ref`), between years (`periods`, which may combine an
observed and a forecast year), or between two forecasts (`y`). With
`groups`, it also separates the composition of a population of subgroups
from the change of their mortality: for groups defined at birth or for
life, such as sex or education, as in Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós
(2024) (`composition = "radix"`); for areas such as deprivation quintiles,
whose populations move between groups, with `composition = "pooled"`, a
parametrisation of this package without a published source.
Forecasts are decomposed draw by draw, so contributions have intervals;
see "Decomposing differences in life expectancy".

## Describing mortality

### How unequal are lifespans?

Life expectancy is the average age at death; `lifespan_variation()` gives
its spread: life disparity (e-dagger), the life-table entropy, the Gini
coefficient, the standard deviation and the interquartile range of the age
at death, from age 0 or conditional on survival to an age `at`. It works
on observed data (with Poisson intervals) and on forecast draws. All
measures depend on the open age interval, e-dagger most: for French women
in 2006 it was 2.1 years higher with an open interval from 85 than with
single years of age to 100+. Use data with an open interval from 95 or
higher, and compare measures only between tables with the same open age.
See "Lifespan variation".

### How do I estimate excess deaths?

Fit a baseline model to the years before the shock and compare the
observed deaths with its predictive draws for the later years:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ex <- mt_excess(lee_carter(), data, baseline = c(2010, 2019), ages = c(0, 65, 80))
mt_plot_excess(ex, type = "p_score")
```

The intervals contain the uncertainty of the baseline trend and the
random variation of the death counts. The result depends on the baseline
model and years, which are assumptions to state; compare a few in the
same call. See "Excess mortality".

## Practicalities

### Are forecasts reproducible?

Yes, with a `seed` (`mt_forecast(..., seed = 1)`, `mt_backtest(..., seed =
1)`). Backtests and `recalibrated()` seed every origin separately, so their
results do not depend on `cores`. Fits of several strata in parallel
(`mt_fit(..., cores = )`) run in forked processes; for models with random
steps in the fit, set `RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")` and a seed before the call
to make them reproducible.

### How long does it take?

Lee-Carter, Li-Lee and random walks fit in seconds even for hundreds of
strata. One-dimensional PCLM ungrouping takes about two seconds per stratum
for 30 years of single ages; the two-dimensional version is much slower.
`apc_bayes()` runs MCMC chains: with `mcmc_control("fast")` from about
ten seconds (8 age groups, 10 years) to one or two minutes per stratum (19
age groups, 14 years).

### Where do the validation numbers come from?

The `validation/` directory of the source repository runs benchmarks with
thresholds on every change (ungrouping accuracy, interval calibration,
coherence). The vignette "Comparison with demography, bamp and StMoMo"
reports accuracy and interval coverage of the models on four data sets.
